note: Round 4b gap research, group C (2026-11-03). Every URL was fetched and checked for the passage described in 'where'. The shared web-search budget ran out partway through, so later candidates came from known sources, verified by direct fetch. Statements some-domains-free-of-ai, building-superhuman-ai-wrong and ai-can-be-real-companion are still under target.

people.name: Candice L. Odgers
people.niche: Developmental psychologist (UC Irvine); leading academic critic of the social-media-causes-teen-mental-illness thesis
people.reason: Her Nature review of The Anxious Generation says the claim that digital technology is causing an epidemic of mental illness 'is not supported by science'.
people.gap: Nobody on the map rejects attention-tech-harms-minds; she is the most prominent research voice on that side.

people.name: Christopher J. Ferguson
people.niche: Psychologist (Stetson University); media-effects and moral-panic researcher
people.reason: He writes that the evidence that social media causes youth mental health problems remains weak, citing his own meta-analyses.
people.gap: A second empirical rejecter of attention-tech-harms-minds, writing from outside the Haidt-Twenge camp.
people.flag: His meta-analysis methods are disputed by Haidt and Rausch; the stance itself is clear.

people.name: Taylor Barkley
people.niche: Tech policy, Abundance Institute; pro-innovation, parental-choice framing
people.reason: His op-ed argues that the GUARD Act's ban on AI companions for minors won't keep kids safe and takes parents out of the decision.
people.gap: Nobody on the map rejects restrict-ai-companions-for-children.

people.name: Elizabeth Nolan Brown
people.niche: Senior editor, Reason; civil-libertarian writer on speech, sex and online regulation
people.reason: She argues the GUARD Act's ban on AI companions for minors is overbroad, overrides parents, and would bring ID checks across the web.
people.gap: A civil-libertarian (privacy and speech) rejecter of restrict-ai-companions-for-children, alongside Barkley's market and parental framing.
people.flag: Journalist; the work is her own-byline opinion analysis, not news reporting about someone else.

people.name: Eugenia Kuyda
people.niche: Founder and CEO of Replika, the AI-companion app
people.reason: She describes Replika as 'an AI friend' and defends AI friendship as a real, if different, kind of relationship, comparing it to a therapist or a pet.
people.gap: Only two figures on the map hold ai-can-be-real-companion; she is the industry's leading voice for it.
people.flag: Commercial interest: she sells AI companions.

people.name: Erik Hoel
people.niche: Neuroscientist and novelist; The Intrinsic Perspective newsletter
people.reason: In 'We need a Butlerian Jihad against AI' he argues that 'strong AI is immoral just in its existence', an abomination, apart from its risks.
people.gap: Only Paul Kingsnorth holds building-superhuman-ai-wrong; Hoel states the in-itself view in secular terms.

people.name: Richard Sutton
people.niche: Reinforcement-learning pioneer, 2024 Turing Award winner; advocate of 'AI succession'
people.reason: He says succession to digital intelligence is inevitable and encourages people to welcome it as a great transition of the universe and to see AIs as our offspring.
people.gap: Only three figures reject human-end-of-ai; Sutton is the most eminent scientist on that side.

people.name: Daniel Faggella
people.niche: Founder of Emerj; 'Worthy Successor' / posthuman-values writer
people.reason: He argues that the great moral aim of AGI should be a 'Worthy Successor' that, rather than humanity, determines the future of life.
people.gap: A second explicit rejecter of human-end-of-ai, framed as a moral goal rather than a forecast.
people.flag: He now disowns the label 'successionism' and calls for slowing down; the essay still argues humanity should not steer forever.

people.name: Joanna J. Bryson
people.niche: Professor of Ethics and Technology, Hertie School; author of 'Robots Should Be Slaves'
people.reason: In testimony to UK parliamentary groups she argues that AI artefacts should not be given moral or legal agency and that robot rights are the wrong frame.
people.gap: Only two figures reject ai-moral-status; she is the field's best-known opponent of AI rights.

people.name: Abeba Birhane
people.niche: Cognitive scientist and AI accountability researcher (Trinity College Dublin)
people.reason: Her paper argues robots are not the kind of thing that could be granted rights at all, and that the debate distracts from human welfare.
people.gap: A decolonial and AI-ethics voice against ai-moral-status, unlike Bryson's legal-design framing.

people.name: Felix M. Simon
people.niche: Communication researcher (Oxford Internet Institute / Reuters Institute) on AI and news
people.reason: He is lead author of an HKS Misinformation Review commentary arguing that fears about generative AI's effect on misinformation are overblown.
people.gap: Adds an empirical media-research voice that rejects ai-threatens-shared-truth.
people.flag: Co-authored with Sacha Altay and Hugo Mercier; attributed to Simon as first author.

works.title: The great rewiring: is social media really behind an epidemic of teenage mental illness?

works.title: Social Media and Youth Mental Health

works.title: From my WhatsApp

works.note: Short post. Cowen allows some harm to girls but says it is much smaller than claimed, so readers may code it as a weak reject or mixed. His 2024 Conversations with Tyler episode with Haidt is stronger, but the page could not be fetched (403/404).

works.author: taylor-barkley
works.title: False GUARD: Banning kids from AI won't keep them safe

statements.where: 'By banning children from the safer AI tools, Congress isn't protecting them'; closing 'not less AI for kids, it should be safer AI'

works.note: He opposes a statutory ban and favours parental choice and safer design. He does not rule out every possible legal rule.

works.title: How a Bill Banning AI Companions for Kids Could Usher in Widespread ID Checks Online

statements.where: 'It takes away their right to talk to AI companions about any topic'; 'Parents would have no ability to opt their kids out'

works.note: Opinion analysis under her byline. Her objections are about parental rights, privacy and speech.

works.author: eugenia-kuyda
works.title: Replika CEO Eugenia Kuyda says it's okay if we end up marrying AI chatbots (Decoder interview)

statements.where: early: 'Replika is an AI friend'; mid: 'AI friends are just another type of that, a completely different type' (therapist/dog comparison)

works.note: The Q&A transcript marks speakers by bolded questions; the labels are lost in a plain-text dump. She says AI friendship has different boundaries from human friendship, but treats it as a real relationship.

works.author: dean-ball
works.title: What's up with the States?

statements.where: section on Nevada's AI mental-health law: mocks 'only a human could ever do mental healthcare'; 'is it better that they talk to a low-cost chatbot, or no one at all?'

works.note: His case against walling off one domain (mental healthcare) where AI may help. A narrow example, not a general principle, so readers may code it as a partial reject.

works.author: erik-hoel
works.title: We need a Butlerian Jihad against AI

statements.where: middle: 'strong AI is immoral in and of itself ... immoral just in its existence ... an abomination'; close: 'Thou shalt not make a machine in the likeness of a human mind'

works.note: Clear in-itself argument, explicitly set against expected-value and risk arguments. It targets 'strong AI' (human-like minds) and does not say 'smarter than humans' in so many words.

works.author: arvind-narayanan
works.title: We Looked at 78 Election Deepfakes. Political Misinformation is not an AI Problem.

statements.where: title and findings list: deceptive AI content 'cheap to replicate without AI'; 'focusing on the demand for misinformation rather than the supply'

works.note: Co-authored with Sayash Kapoor and attributed to the on-map Narayanan. They grant real dangers (NCII, the liar's dividend), so this is a reject with caveats. Same post also at normaltech.ai.

works.author: felix-simon
works.title: Misinformation reloaded? Fears about the impact of generative AI on misinformation are overblown

statements.where: abstract: 'current concerns about the effects of generative AI on the misinformation landscape are overblown'

works.note: Three authors (Simon, Altay, Mercier). Drop it if co-authored commentary is out of scope.

works.author: richard-sutton
works.title: Richard Sutton: Father of RL thinks LLMs are a dead end

statements.where: section '00:53:48 Succession to AI': 'succession to digital intelligence ... is inevitable'; 'I do encourage people to think positively about it'; AIs as 'our offspring'

works.note: Speaker-labelled transcript. He frames succession as a stage of the universe and leaves room for good and bad outcomes. The section may also bear on ai-moral-status.

works.author: daniel-faggella
works.title: A Worthy Successor: The Purpose of AGI

statements.where: core definition: 'the great moral aim of AGI ... should be the creation of Worthy Successor'; 'the expanding process won't center on us, and shouldn't eternally be steered by us'

works.note: Updated 2026-10-15 with an opening note disowning 'successionism' and favouring a slowdown. The thesis that humanity is not the permanent end still stands.

works.author: robin-hanson
works.title: Who Are Your Descendants?

statements.where: opening: 'future AIs are our descendants, not co-existing rivals'; evolved 'indulgence of descendants, even when different from you'

works.note: Hanson argues we should treat AIs as literal descendants to indulge, not keep humanity fixed as the end. Backup: 'AI Fear Is Mostly Fear Of Future' (overcomingbias.com/p/ai-fear-is-mostly-fear-of-future, 2023-04-13), on unaligned descendants being the default.

works.author: scott-alexander
works.title: Should The Future Be Human?

statements.where: section III: 'Maybe the future should be human, and maybe it shouldn't'; 'a successor species we can be proud of'; 'I would be most willing to accept being replaced by AI if...'

works.note: Mixed, so readers may code it as unclear. He is open in principle to an AI successor under conditions (consciousness, individuation, no force), but also writes 'humans uber alles' about alien conquest. Include only if a conditional reject counts.

works.author: joanna-bryson
works.title: Why AI is amoral, and artefacts can't consent
works.channel: Adventures in NI (blog); notes for testimony to UK APPGs on 'The Rights of Robots'

statements.where: recommendation section: attributing 'moral or legal agency' to AI products would make 'perfect shell companies'; rebuttal to the 'same moral patiency' objection: 'ban it ... or offer it the same protections as any work of art'

works.note: Her argument is normative and rests on design, not on AI lacking consciousness: artefacts should never be made moral patients or agents. Her 2017 post 'Why Robots (and Animals) Never Need Rights' says the same.

works.author: abeba-birhane
works.title: Robot Rights? Let's Talk about Human Welfare Instead

statements.where: abstract: 'deny that robots ... are the kinds of things that could be granted rights in the first place'

works.note: Co-authored with Jelle van Dijk. The abstract page states the thesis plainly.
